chunks: "A servo is precise because it never trusts the motor.
It measures where the shaft actually is, compares that to the command, and keeps correcting until the error is basically zero.
So the precision of the motion is set by the sensor and the loop, not by how well the motor behaves. A few things make that work well.

First, a high-resolution sensor: a hobby servo's potentiometer gives a fraction of a degree, but an industrial encoder gives thousands to millions of counts per turn, so a 17-bit absolute encoder resolves about 0.
003 degrees. Second, gearing: if the encoder is on the motor and there's a 10:1 gearbox, everything gets ten times finer at the output.
Third, the loop itself: high proportional gain makes it stiff, so a load pushing on it barely moves it, and an integral term pushes the steady-state error to zero even under a constant load.
The caveat is that resolution isn't accuracy.
Backlash in the gears, flex in the shaft, sensor non-linearity, friction and noise all limit what you really get, particularly if the sensor is on the motor and the error is out at the load."
